props.title: An American Tail
props.initialSlug: A brave mouse seeks his family in 1880s America

sections.content: An American Tail revolutionized animated storytelling by tackling serious historical themes through the lens of immigrant mice. Don Bluth, fresh from leaving Disney, crafted this ambitious tale that dared to address anti-Semitism, poverty, and the immigrant experience in late 1800s America. The film's haunting "Somewhere Out There" sequence influenced emotional storytelling in animation, paving the way for powerful musical moments in later works like The Lion King (1994) and Coco (2017). Bluth's distinctive animation style - characterized by fluid movement and darker themes - provided a stark contrast to Disney's output of the era.

sections.content: The success of An American Tail marked a crucial moment in animation history, proving audiences would embrace more complex narratives. The film's $47 million domestic box office challenged Disney's dominance and helped spark the animation renaissance of the late 1980s and 1990s. This competition pushed Disney to innovate, leading to The Little Mermaid (1989) and their subsequent renaissance. Bluth's emphasis on emotional depth and historical context influenced later immigrant narratives in animation like Persepolis (2007) and An American Tail: Fievel Goes West (1991). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Animation

The film's blend of historical events with accessible characters created a template for addressing serious topics in family animation. This influence can be seen in works like Zootopia (2016), which uses animal characters to explore discrimination, and Wolfwalkers (2020), which tackles historical persecution through folklore. The character of Fievel Mousekewitz became an iconic figure in animation, with his blue hat and optimistic spirit inspiring characters in films like Ratatouille (2007) and The Tale of Despereaux (2008).
